{"id": "26:197/q04", "question": "What is the sign in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether 'sign' names the scholars' recognition, the Qur'an or Prophet recognized, or a particular scholar's belief.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q04/p1", "position": "Israelite scholars' knowledge or recognition is the sign confirming the Qur'an's truth and Muhammad's prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says their knowledge of the Qur'an's truth confirms Muhammad as messenger. Al-Zajjaj cites his description in Torah and Gospel. Al-Qurtubi and al-Biqa'i say Quraysh trusted the People of the Book for religious reports. Al-Biqa'i adds Torah, Gospel, Psalms and other books; their alteration did not cancel their evidentiary value for adherents. Ibn Ashur calls this a third commendation of the Qur'an; al-Tabataba'i says Jews used their predictions to claim advantage over Arabs. Islahi says opponents thereby lack a further excuse and describes their selective trust in supportive unbelievers. The sign can attest either Qur'an or prophethood, as al-Baydawi explicitly says."}, {"id": "26:197/q04/p2", "position": "The Qur'an itself is the sign.", "reasons": "Mubashshir ibn Ubayd gives this identification in both Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Durr."}, {"id": "26:197/q04/p3", "position": "Muhammad himself is the sign, recognized from the earlier scriptures.", "reasons": "Qatada says the Prophet was the sign and that Israelite scholars recognized his scriptural description."}, {"id": "26:197/q04/p4", "position": "Abd Allah ibn Salam's belief in Muhammad's Book exemplifies the intended sign.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas calls him one of Israel's best scholars; his acceptance of the Book witnesses to its truth."}]}
{"id": "26:197/q05", "question": "How are 'was' and 'sign' read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted consonant of the verb and case ending of āya.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q05/p1", "position": "The majority read masculine yakun and accusative āyatan.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi lists Ibn Amir alone against the other readers; Ibn al-Jawzi names Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu Amr, Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i for this form. Qiraat-ER labels yakun canonical, and al-Durr reports Asim's ya reading. Ibn Atiyya also reports Ibn Masud and al-A'mash have another wording and Ubay's codex omits the opening waw, without supplying their exact wording."}, {"id": "26:197/q05/p2", "position": "Ibn Amir and other reported readers read feminine takun and nominative āyatun.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add al-Jahdari; Ibn al-Jawzi adds Ibn Abi Abla. Some of Ibn Atiyya's readers of masculine yakun also raise āya. Yahya says this reading makes the sign a subject."}, {"id": "26:197/q05/p3", "position": "Some read feminine takun while keeping āyatan accusative.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this to Abu Imran al-Jawni and Qatada; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi report it from Ibn Abbas."}]}
{"id": "26:197/q06", "question": "How is the clause involving 'was a sign' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether kāna is complete, which expression supplies its subject and predicate, and whether feminine agreement follows grammar or meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q06/p1", "position": "With masculine yakun and accusative āyatan, the infinitive clause is the subject and āyatan the advanced predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh says the scholars' knowledge is definite; al-Samin says lahum is circumstantial to āya. Bursevi says fronting emphasizes the sign. Al-Burhan gives a pronoun-of-affair explanation for the cited reading."}, {"id": "26:197/q06/p2", "position": "With feminine takun and nominative āya, āya is subject and the scholars' knowledge clause is predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh, al-Zajjaj, al-Qurtubi, al-Biqa'i and others give this direct analysis. Al-Zamakhshari, as reported by Abu Hayyan, finds an indefinite subject before a definite predicate awkward; al-Samin says this is unnecessary and rejects its defense as poetic necessity. Al-Alusi calls the order weak."}, {"id": "26:197/q06/p3", "position": "A feminine verb can contain an implicit story or affair pronoun, with the following clause explaining it.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi cites 21:97 and 22:46 for feminine agreement with a feminine expression within the explanatory clause. Al-Wahidi and al-Tabrisi report the implicit story; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Samin give affair-pronoun versions. Al-Samin varies the placement of lahum and āya."}, {"id": "26:197/q06/p4", "position": "The infinitive clause itself is raised by feminine takun because its meaning is the feminine 'sign'.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi, al-Wahidi and Abu Ali in al-Tabrisi cite semantic agreement; they compare 6:160 and a reading of 6:23."}, {"id": "26:197/q06/p5", "position": "Feminine takun can be a complete verb, with āya its subject and the knowledge clause apposition or an omitted subject's predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi mentions complete kāna; al-Samin says lahum attaches to it. Al-Baydawi and al-Samin also give an incomplete-verb parse with lahum predicate, āya subject, and the clause appositive or supplied predicate."}, {"id": "26:197/q06/p6", "position": "Feminine takun with accusative āyatan uses agreement by meaning, with a feminine predicate or understood verbal noun.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj compares 6:23; Abu Hayyan allows agreement with the predicate or construed feminine noun; al-Samin cites 6:23 and poetry; al-Alusi cites Labid's wild-ass verse and rejects deriving agreement from the genitive noun because the usual condition is absent."}]}
{"id": "26:197/q07", "question": "What does the object pronoun in 'know it' refer to?", "turns_on": "Which nearby discourse item the singular object pronoun resumes.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q07/p1", "position": "The Qur'an, its mention, or its described qualities in prior scripture.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi explicitly prefers the Qur'an; Ibn Ashur says it may mean knowing its mention. Ibn Ashur permits the preceding claim of its presence in earlier writings, referring to 26:196."}]}
{"id": "26:197/q08", "question": "What did the Israelite scholars know?", "turns_on": "Whether the knowledge centers on Muhammad's predicted attributes, the Qur'an, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q08/p1", "position": "Their scriptures described Muhammad, his time, mission, and prophetic qualities.", "reasons": "Qatada says Torah and Gospel name him as God's Messenger; reports from Jews say the Torah describes him and his time. Ibn Ashur adds verification that the bearer actually matches those qualities. Islahi says most concealed these predictions. Al-Tabataba'i says Jewish communities used them for glad tidings and advantage over Arabs."}, {"id": "26:197/q08/p2", "position": "Their books foretold the Qur'an's advent or contained its described qualities and teachings.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the earlier-scripture wording is general in form but concerns some books revealed to some messengers. {"id": "26:197/q09", "question": "Is the verb 'know it' read in masculine or feminine form?", "turns_on": "Whether agreement follows the masculine plural scholars or a feminine collective interpretation of Banu Israel.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q09/p1", "position": "The usual reading is masculine yaʿlamahu.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it the majority's reading in contrast to al-Jahdari's taʿlamahu."}, {"id": "26:197/q09/p2", "position": "Al-Jahdari and others read feminine taʿlamahu.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi also names al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak. {"id": "26:197/q13", "question": "What consultation of Jewish scholars is reported behind this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the consulted rabbis plainly confirmed Muhammad or gave a confused answer.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q13/p1", "position": "Meccans asked Jews in Medina or Yathrib about Muhammad; they said his time had come and the Torah described him, confirming his truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is the recurring transmitter; Kuran Yolu says emissaries were sent and Study Quran reports the answer from at least some People of the Book. {"id": "26:197/q14", "question": "What effect did Israelite testimony have among the Arabs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q14/p1", "position": "Their scriptural reports and predictions helped bring the Aws and Khazraj to Islam.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi reports this with Ibn Abbas's identification of Ibn Salam and companions, and says Israelites told Arabs of the Qur'an's mention and foretold the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "26:197/q15", "question": "Was this verse revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Whether mention of Israelite scholars, especially later converts, requires a Medinan setting or fits the Meccan context and reported consultation.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q15/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, in line with the sura's setting and a prior Jewish consultation report.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya prefers Meccan and says the Torah already described the unlettered Prophet; Abu Hayyan prefers the Meccan setting for the occasion report; al-Alusi says context and that report support it. {"id": "26:197/q16", "question": "How does this verse connect with the preceding passage and sura?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q16/p1", "position": "It confirms the prior statement that earlier writings attest the Qur'an and adds a fresh commendation of it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls it the third commendation and says the conjunction signals a new commendation as well as supporting evidence; if it were merely evidence, coordination would be unexpected. {"id": "26:197/q20", "question": "What are the biographical reports about early reciters here?", "turns_on": "The reports concern different people and incidents.", "positions": [{"id": "26:197/q20/p1", "position": "Abu Ja'far and Shayba were linked through Medina recitation teaching and Shayba's marriage to Abu Ja'far's daughter.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid dates al-Harra fifty-three years after the Prophet's death. Al-Mufaddal says Shayba led Sukayna's funeral prayer."}, {"id": "26:197/q20/p2", "position": "A mark seen on Abu Ja'far after death was taken for the light of the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Nafi reports a page-like mark between his neck and heart observed by those washing him."}, {"id": "26:197/q20/p3", "position": "Muslim ibn Jundab was an eloquent Medinan preacher who reported from al-Zubayr and Ibn Umar.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid supplies these biographical details."}]}

{"id": "27:7/q02", "question": "Whom does Moses call his family?", "turns_on": "Whether ahl and the plural address designate only the wife or other companions, especially children, as well.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q02/p1", "position": "His wife, Shuʿayb's daughter, is the family member addressed; some accounts say she alone accompanied him.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Zajjāj identify his wife; al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya name Shuʿayb's daughter. {"id": "27:7/q03", "question": "Why does Moses address his family in the plural?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural is a manner of addressing one wife or counts other hearers.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q03/p1", "position": "One wife can be addressed as a group or honorifically.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Kashshāf report the wife-alone explanation. {"id": "27:7/q04", "question": "What circumstances brought Moses to the fire?", "turns_on": "The first answer recounts the journey's practical circumstances; the second emphasizes its prophetic outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q04/p1", "position": "Traveling from Midian toward Egypt, Moses lost the road on a cold dark night; his fire-making failed, so he sought directions and warmth.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says his flint failed; Ibn ʿAbbās says he had completed his term. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds rain, lost fire, and failed fire-sticks. Bursevī reports his wife in labor and a fire by the Mount; al-Ālūsī specifies Wadi Ṭuwā, and Elmâlılı says all means had failed. Al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Iṣlāḥī and Kur'an Yolu give variants of the same journey."}, {"id": "27:7/q04/p2", "position": "Moses found the fire at the place where divine calling and prophecy awaited him.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim presents the lost road as the setting for divine honor, prophecy and speech. Ibn Kathīr places the fire by the Mount and says Moses returned with momentous news and great light; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the utterance immediately prepares for the call in 27:8."}]}
{"id": "27:7/q05", "question": "What does آنست mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb merely states sensory perception or also conveys reassurance and familiarity.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q05/p1", "position": "Moses saw or perceived a fire.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda links ins to what is visible; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites a line of Ḥassān, and al-Qurṭubī a line of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza. Al-Rāzī prefers seeing because Arabic does not distinguish perceived with my eye from saw with my eye. Bursevī's Tāj relates the root to appearance and the departure of estrangement; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes subtle sensory noticing by sight or hearing."}, {"id": "27:7/q05/p2", "position": "Moses sensed or encountered the fire in a reassuring, familiar way.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Jishumī stress perception with familiarity or calm; al-Rāzī reports coming upon the fire and feeling familiarity. {"id": "27:7/q06", "question": "What was the fire Moses perceived?", "turns_on": "Whether the apparent fire is identified as divine light or only described as it appeared to Moses.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q06/p1", "position": "It appeared to be fire but was divine light.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it the light of the Lord of Majesty, seen Friday night on the mountain's right in the Holy Land; Bursevī repeats him. {"id": "27:7/q09", "question": "What does the future prefix in سآتيكم convey?", "turns_on": "Whether sīn chiefly strengthens the assurance or marks distance and expected delay; several sources combine them.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q09/p1", "position": "It assures his family that he will return with something, even if delayed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and al-Bayḍāwī treat sīn as strengthening a promise. {"id": "27:7/q16", "question": "What does قبس mean and why is it paired with شهاب?", "turns_on": "The first is the concrete object sought here; the second is a cited extension of the same root.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q16/p1", "position": "Fire or a flame taken from another fire, especially a live ember or brand to kindle or carry warmth.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Naḥḥās, al-Māwardī, al-Jishumī and many others define taken fire. {"id": "27:7/q17", "question": "How is شهاب قبس read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The reading's tanwīn and whether qabas is adjective, apposition, noun for a distinct firebrand, verbal noun, or an allegedly self-annexed synonymous name. {"id": "27:7/q25", "question": "What does this episode contribute to the sūra's presentation of revelation and prophecy?", "turns_on": "These sources emphasize different implications of the same episode: divine wisdom, prophetic consolation, divine training, sura pattern, or expressive density.", "positions": [{"id": "27:7/q25/p1", "position": "Moses' encounter displays God's knowledge and wisdom and parallels Muḥammad's receipt of revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī treat it as another sign of divine knowledge; al-Biqāʿī says the ordered stories demonstrate perfect wisdom and knowledge and counter claims that the Qur'an is human or exhaustible.
